nba_directive.reason_text: This client has a 2.75% VA loan — one of the lowest rates in existence — so a cash-out refi would destroy their payment and rate; the play is to honor their 'revisit later' stance while making the cost of waiting concrete and pinning a real callback before they go cold.
nba_directive.recommended_strategy_text:
- Open by acknowledging their timeline AND immediately anchoring to their specific loan position
  - Name their 2.75% VA rate explicitly: 'You have one of the best rates out there — we are absolutely not touching that first mortgage'
  - This builds trust and signals you are protecting their interest, not just selling

- Quantify the cost of waiting in real dollars tied to their stated life goal
  - Their remaining balance is $158,552 — ask them to confirm the goal (retirement runway, debt payoff, a specific purchase or event) so the scenario is personalized, not generic
  - If they have high-rate debt (credit cards at 25–30%), calculate what they are paying monthly on those balances right now and contrast that against a HELOC rate — this is the number that makes waiting expensive
  - Frame it: 'Every month you wait is another [X dollars] in credit-card interest you are paying that a HELOC could eliminate — let me run that exact figure for you'

- Reframe the product clearly: HELOC / second lien, not a cash-out refi
  - 'We would put a second lien behind your 2.75% VA loan — your $735/month payment stays exactly where it is'
  - Position the HELOC rate against their credit-card rates (25–30%), not against their mortgage rate — that is the correct comparison

- Honor the delay but make it concrete — pin a callback before ending the conversation
  - Do not accept a vague 'check back later' — offer two specific times: 'Can we do a 10-minute call Tuesday at 10am or Thursday at 2pm?'
  - Confirm the callback in writing via text immediately after they agree
  - Note: single-attempt-then-silence is the conversion killer here — the pinned time is non-negotiable

- Leave them with one clean reframe to carry into the waiting period
  - 'If rates drop later, you can always refinance the HELOC or roll it in — you are not locked in forever. Right now the question is how much high-rate debt you want to keep paying while you wait.'
